shippingNews.postTitle: Gaia Desgagnes Makes Unusual Trip to Lake Superior

stories.body: Tanker Gaia Desgagnes headed for the Soo Locks Monday morning. [Roger LeLievre] The Canadian-flagged Tanker Gaia Desgagnes was upbound at the Soo Locks late Monday morning headed for Thunder Bay, ON, with a cargo of diesel. This is a rare trip for the 2018-built vessel, which is owned by Groupe Desgagnes, Quebec City.

shippingNews.postTitle: Duluth Ship Fans Welcome Visiting R/V Neil Armstrong

stories.body: DULUTH, MN – The R/V Neil Armstrong arrived at Duluth Monday morning from its home port of Woods Hole, MA. The University of Minnesota Duluth is working with the research vessel to detect and observe neutrino interactions in Lake Superior. Neutrinos are the most abundant particles that have mass in the universe, and they pass through everything. They are very difficult to detect, so studying them requires special instruments. todayInHistory.title: Life Aboard the Edmund Fitzgerald Described in Letters from Cadet
todayInHistory.text: David "Cowboy" Weiss in 1974. [GLSHS] DETROIT, MI – It wasn't just the hat that earned Edmund Fitzgerald crew member David Weiss his nickname "Cowboy." It was his friend and Great Lakes Maritime Academy classmate David James, who had just watched Frank Zappa's 1971 movie "200 Motels" featuring the character Lonesome Cowboy Burt. When James saw Weiss standing outside a classroom dressed in black and wearing a cowboy hat, the nickname came easily."He looked a little different," James said. Weiss was less "bummy" than the rest of their classmates, who dressed to emulate the sailors they were training to join. The day they met, James gave Weiss his nickname "Cowboy Burt." DuMouchelles auction house in downtown Detroit is selling letters written by a man killed in the Edmund Fitzgerald sinking in Lake Superior on Nov. 10, 1975. The letters were written by David Weiss while he was on the Fitzgerald. The friendship between Weiss and James is chronicled in a series of letters they exchanged while out on the inland seas in 1975, when Weiss was on the Edmund Fitzgerald and James on the Walter A. Sterling. The last was sent Oct. 30, about two weeks before Weiss went down with the Edmund Fitzgerald during a storm in Lake Superior. Twenty-eight crewmates perished along with him. todayInHistory.title: Maritime Historian Valerie van Heest to Speak In Ludington
todayInHistory.text: LUDINGTON, MI – Maritime historian, author and shipwreck explorer Valerie van Heest, whose work has helped shape the visitor experience at all three Mason County Historical Society museums, will be the featured speaker at the society’s annual dinner meeting Thursday, Dec. 3. Maritime Historian Valerie van Heest. [Mason County Historical Society] Van Heest, one of Michigan’s leading maritime historians and shipwreck researchers, will present “History of the Great Lakes,” based on her new book, “A History of the Great Lakes in Twelve Shipwrecks.” The program will explore 250 years of Great Lakes history through a dozen shipwrecks, showing how these underwater discoveries reveal broader stories of conflict, settlement, innovation and change. The annual meeting will take place at the United Methodist Church of Ludington, 5810 Bryant Road. Doors will open at 5:45 p.m., with dinner beginning at 6 p.m. The society’s annual business meeting and organizational updates will follow dinner, and van Heest’s presentation will begin at 7:30 p.m. Van Heest is co-founder and president of the Michigan Shipwreck Research Association and has helped discover about 20 shipwrecks off Michigan’s west coast while participating in archaeological investigations at more than 50 shipwreck sites throughout the Great Lakes. marineWeather.synopsis: A 29.7 inch low over eastern Ontario will track east today as another low at 29.9 inches approaches the Northern Plains from Alberta. This low will deepen to 29.7 inches as it moves south of the area, to southern Lake Michigan by Wednesday afternoon and then on to the Eastern Great Lakes Wednesday night. Thereafter Lake Superior will be between a 30.2 inch high over the Northern Plains and a 29.5 inch low over the Northeast. The high shifts east, over Lake Superior and builds to 30.4 inches on Sunday.

A weak low pressure trough around 30.0 inches will swing across Lake Michigan this morning, bringing a brief period of gusty northwest winds. Look for winds to diminish this afternoon as high pressure around 30.1 inches builds into the region. Light and variable winds are expected through Wednesday morning before becoming northeasterly Wednesday afternoon as low pressure deepens to 29.6 inches in Illinois/Indiana. Winds increase and become northerly through Wednesday night into Thursday, with gales likely Thursday as low pressure moves into the mid-Atlantic and continues to deepen to 29.4 inches. Anticipating the need for Gale Watches by this afternoon. Winds gradually turn northwesterly and diminish Friday night as low pressure exits into the Atlantic Ocean. Also Wednesday night through Friday, a band of lake effect rain/snow showers will develop. Locally reduced visibilities are expected throughout this timeframe.

Low pressure swings from Ontario into Quebec during the morning hours as its attendant dry cold front crosses the central Great Lakes. High pressure arrives by Wednesday, but gets displaced by surface low pressure digging into the Ohio Valley Wednesday night. Showers, with potential for mixed precipitation, linger into the weekend as larger scale troughing persists.

Pressure persists averaging 30.00 inches ahead of a cold front that will cross Lake Erie Wednesday night into Thursday, as low pressure 29.80 inches tracks south of the lake during that time. Troughing 30.00 inches will linger across the eastern Great Lakes on Friday as low pressure exits off the east coast.

A 29.6 inch low will move across southern Quebec today before reaching the Gulf of Maine by Wednesday. A weak ridge averaging 29.9 inches will build across the lower Great Lakes tonight through Wednesday. Another 29.5 inch low will move into the Ohio Valley Wednesday night, then give way to a secondary low along the Mid Atlantic coast on Thursday. This 29.2 inch coastal low will move northeast and offshore of the New England coast Friday through Saturday before reaching the Canadian Maritimes Saturday night.
